title: Most Copies With a Raise Budget
statement:
You get an array nums and a budget k. One operation picks any element and raises it by 1. Values can never go down. You may do at most k operations in total, spread over any elements.

After the operations, some value appears more often than any other. Return the largest number of copies of a single value you can reach.

examples.why: Raise 3 to 4 (1 step) and 2 to 4 (2 steps). Now 4 appears three times. Reaching 9 would cost far more than 3.
With no budget the two 7s already count. The 8 cannot be lowered to 7.
Raise the 4 to 5. The cheapest copies to make are the values just below the target, not the smallest ones.

hints: Which value should the copies end up as? Could the target ever be something that is not already in the array?
Sort the array. If the target is nums[r], the cheapest elements to raise are the ones right below it, so the copies form a contiguous block ending at r.
Slide a window over the sorted array. Raising the window [l..r] to nums[r] costs (r − l + 1) · nums[r] − sum(window). While that exceeds k, drop nums[l].

explain.intuition:
Raising a value past every element you are copying is wasted budget, so the target is always one of the existing values. Once the array is sorted and the target is nums[r], the cheapest elements to raise are its nearest smaller neighbours, because each one needs the fewest steps. So the best group for that target is a contiguous block of the sorted array that ends at r.

The cost of lifting a block to its last value is size · nums[r] − sum. When r moves right, the target grows, so the cost of keeping the same left end only grows. That is the shape a sliding window needs: extend on the right, shrink on the left while the block is too expensive.
steps: Keep a window [l..r] and its running sum.
While (r − l + 1) · nums[r] − sum > k, subtract nums[l] and move l right.
Record r − l + 1 as a candidate and return the largest.
pitfalls: Picking the most frequent value as the target. In [1, 4, 5, 5] it happens to work, but in [1, 2, 3, 10] with k = 3 the right target is 3, which appears once.
Raising the smallest elements first instead of the ones nearest the target. The block must be contiguous in sorted order.
Overflow in fixed-width languages: size · nums[r] reaches 1010, so use 64-bit integers.

complexity.time: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the window

solutions.title: Grow leftwards from every target
solutions.idea: Sort, then for each target nums[r] walk left, paying nums[r] − nums[l] for each element, until the budget runs out.

solutions.title: Sort + sliding window
solutions.idea: The cost of lifting a sorted window to its right end is size · nums[r] − sum. Shrink from the left while it exceeds k.

followups: Why does the window never need to shrink by more than one step per new r if you only care about the maximum size?
Solve it with prefix sums and a binary search on the left end for each r. Which version is easier to get right?
